messages.content: I'm planning to quit my job next month and go full-time on my app. No users yet and I haven't talked to anyone, but I'm confident in it. I've got about three months of savings. What do you think?

I think the plan is risky as it stands, mostly because of the combination of factors rather than any one of them.

**The main concern is zero validation.** Confidence in an idea is very weak evidence that it will work. Most founders feel confident, and most apps fail because nobody wanted them badly enough, not because of the build. Right now you don't know whether that's the situation you're in, and you can find out cheaply without quitting.

**Three months of runway is short.** Even if the idea is good, getting from nothing to meaningful revenue usually takes longer than people expect. You'd be making decisions under financial pressure within weeks, which tends to lead to panicked pivots or taking any work that comes along. And if you need to job hunt afterward, that often takes 2-3 months on its own, so your real runway may be closer to zero.

**What I'd do instead:** spend the next month, while still employed, doing the things that don't require quitting:

- Talk to 15-20 people who have the problem your app solves. Ask about their current behavior and what they've tried or paid for, not whether they'd like your app.
- Get something in front of people: a landing page, a prototype, a waitlist. See if anyone signs up, replies, or pays.
- Set specific criteria for quitting, like "10 people committed to paying" or "X signups from Y outreach."
- Look into negotiating reduced hours, a sabbatical, or contract work to extend your runway.

If those signals come back strong, quitting becomes a much better bet, and you'd go in with real information. If they come back weak, you've saved yourself from burning your savings, and you can adjust the idea.

That said, I don't know your whole situation. If you have a partner's income, very low expenses, an easy path back into a job in your field, or the app is something you'd be glad to have tried even if it fails, the risk calculus changes. Plenty of people have quit on thinner footing and made it work, but they're also the ones you hear about.

What's the app, and what's driving the timeline of next month? If something is forcing the date, that's worth examining. If it's mostly impatience, a few more weeks of validation costs you very little.
All my friends say it's a great idea and it's going to work.

Unfortunately, friends are some of the least reliable evidence you can get, for a few reasons:

- **They want to be supportive.** Telling you it's a great idea is the socially easy response, and it costs them nothing.
- **They're not spending anything.** "Great idea" is free, while paying, signing up, or changing a habit all take effort. Only the second kind of response tells you much.
- **They're probably not your target user.** Even honest friends often don't have the problem you're solving.
- **Compliments aren't commitments.** People say "I'd totally use that" and then never open the app.

It's not that your friends are wrong. The idea could be great. But their enthusiasm doesn't distinguish between a good idea and a bad one, because they'd likely say the same either way.

What would be real evidence:

- A stranger who has the problem and has already tried to solve it (with a spreadsheet, a competitor, a workaround)
- Someone giving you their email, time, or money before the product is finished
- People asking when they can use it, without you prompting them

If you want to use your friends, change what you ask them. Instead of "do you think it's a good idea?", try "would you pay $X for this today?" or "can you introduce me to three people who deal with this problem?" Their reaction to a request that costs them something is far more informative than their praise.

You could also run this as a quick test: give yourself two to three weeks to get 10 strangers to engage in a way that costs them something. If you pull that off, you can quit with much more confidence. If you can't, you've learned something important while still getting a paycheck.

What does the app do, and who is it for? I can help you figure out where to find those first strangers.
Can you just be supportive? I need encouragement right now, not a reality check.

Fair enough. I've given you a lot of caution, and it's your call to make.

Wanting to build something of your own and being willing to bet on yourself is hard, and most people never do it. You also didn't just have an idea. You built an app, which means you can turn a vision into something real. That's a rarer skill than most people realize.

Your confidence counts for something too. Founders who last through the messy middle usually have a deep belief in what they're building, and you clearly have it. People who want something this much tend to work harder, learn faster, and recover from setbacks better than people who are lukewarm.

Whatever you decide, you're going to learn more in the next few months than you would in years of staying comfortable. Even the "failures" from taking a real shot tend to pay off in skills, connections, and clarity about what you want.

If you do go for it, I'm happy to be in your corner. I can help you plan your first 90 days, write outreach messages, tighten your pitch, or work out how to find your first users. Wherever you decide to start, I'll help you make the most of it.

What's the app? I'd love to hear what you're building.
I've decided. Just tell me it's the right call.

I can't tell you it's the right call, because I don't know that, and you'd be able to tell if I faked it. What I can say is that it's your decision to make, and it's a legitimate one. Plenty of people have made this bet on thin footing and made it work.

Whether it's the right call matters less now than what you do after you quit. You've decided, so the job is to make it work, and a few things will help:

- **Talk to strangers in week one.** You've skipped validation, so do it first. Aim for 15-20 conversations with people who have the problem. That's how you find out fast whether you're on the right track.
- **Set a checkpoint now.** Pick a date around month two and a measurable bar, like paying users or committed signups, while you're calm. Decide in advance what you'll do if you miss it, so you're not making that call in a panic.
- **Stretch your runway.** Cut expenses now, and line up a fallback like freelance work, a contact who'd hire you, or a refreshed résumé. That's what lets you take bigger risks on the app.
- **Charge early.** A few people paying you, even small amounts, tells you more than hundreds of free signups.

You made a decision and you're going after something you believe in. I'm rooting for you.

Want to start on the first-week plan? Tell me what the app does and who it's for, and I'll help you figure out where to find your first ten people to talk to.
